extracted.intended_audience: readers and students of political philosophy; scholars of early modern political theory; general readers of classic texts
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and summarizing Hobbes' normative principles and definitional claims from Leviathan (1651), for use in annotation, study, or secondary analysis of early-modern political theory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common-wealth as an Artificial Man
rubrics_metrics.description: A common-wealth (or State, civitas) is an Artificial Man: the Sovereignty is the artificial soul, magistrates are artificial joints, reward and punishment are the nerves, wealth is the strength — the body politic formed by pacts and covenants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used by Hobbes as the organizing metaphor for thinking about political authority, obligations, and functions; emphasizes unity, artificial construction by human art, and analogy between bodily parts and public institutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generation and Definition of a Common-wealth (by Covenant/Institution)
rubrics_metrics.description: A common-wealth is generated by covenant: men unite under one judgment so as to obtain particular security that natural law and mere multitude cannot provide; the act of instituting a common-wealth is a contract whereby subjects submit to a sovereign.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hobbes sets out the social-contract origin of political authority; the legitimacy of sovereign power derives from the mutual agreement of individuals to transfer rights for protection and peace.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sovereign Rights By Institution (enumerated consequences)
rubrics_metrics.description: Consequences of instituting a common-wealth include: (1) subjects cannot change the form of government; (2) sovereign power cannot be forfeited; (3) subjects cannot justly protest the institution declared by the majority; (4) sovereign's actions cannot be justly accused by subjects; (5) sovereign's acts are unpunishable by subjects; (6) sovereign judges what is necessary for peace and defence and what doctrines are fit to be taught; (7) sovereign makes rules determining ownership and property; (8) sovereign holds all judicature and decision of controversies; (9) sovereign makes war and peace; (10) sovereign chooses counsellors and ministers; (11) sovereign rewards and punishes arbitrarily where no former law decides measure; (12) sovereign grants honour and order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hobbes emphasizes indivisibility of these rights and their centrality to sovereignty; these are presented as the core legal-political powers a sovereign acquires by institution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Forms of Commonwealth
rubrics_metrics.description: There are three different forms of common-wealth by institution: monarchy, aristocracy, and democracy (assembly); differences and dangers (e.g., tyranny, oligarchy) are discussed in relation to relative merits and stability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hobbes compares forms (monarchy vs assemblies), discusses succession, and warns of subordinate representatives and dangers of mixed governments.

rubrics_metrics.name: First and Second Natural Laws and Contracts
rubrics_metrics.description: Natural laws include: (1) seek peace and follow it; (2) lay down a right to all things and be contented with as much liberty as others will allow in mutual covenant — i.e., the foundations for making covenants and renouncing rights for peace.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hobbes formulates the basic principles that justify entering contracts and establishing authority; he also discusses when covenants are valid, when they are void, and the limits on alienability of rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and Rules of Covenants/Contracts
rubrics_metrics.description: Contracts/covenants are mutual promises; contracts may be express or tacit; free gifts pass only by present or past words; covenants extorted by fear are valid; some rights are not alienable; covenants can be voided in certain circumstances (impossibility, coercion, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hobbes gives specific tests and signs of contract formation, explains when covenants bind, and analyzes exceptions (e.g., with beasts, with God without revelation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Person, Author, and Representation
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinction between natural person and artificial person: an actor vs author; covenants made by authority bind the author, not merely the actor; plural voices can make one representative person; personation can be of inanimate or irrational things by convention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key for understanding how collective bodies (sovereign, assemblies) act and are held responsible; treatments of authorship and agency in legal-political acts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Liberty of Subjects
rubrics_metrics.description: Liberty is absence of external impediments to motion; subject's liberty is consistent with fear and necessity; subjects retain liberty to defend their bodies; liberty of subjects consists in freedom from private covenants that contradict sovereign obligations; greatest liberty depends on silence of law; specific cases where subjects may be absolved of obedience (captivity, sovereign casting off government, banishment, sovereign becoming subject to another).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hobbes explains liberty in relation to sovereignty and the limits of individual freedom within political order; includes measures for assessing when disobedience may be justified.

rubrics_metrics.name: Civil Law: Sovereign as Legislator and Requirements of Law
rubrics_metrics.description: The sovereign is the legislator and not subject to civil law; a law is not law if not made known; interpretation of law depends on sovereign power; the authentic interpretation of law is not that of writers but of judges; laws require verification by registers, letters patent, public seals, or judge's sentence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hobbes sets procedural and epistemic criteria for what counts as law and how laws are to be verified and interpreted within the common-wealth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of Crime, Excuses, and Extenuations
rubrics_metrics.description: A crime is an act contrary to civil law; where no civil law exists there is no crime; ignorance of natural law excuses not; ignorance of civil law sometimes excuses; ignorance of sovereign excuses not; ignorance of the penalty excuses not; punishments declared before the fact limit later increases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides normative rules for attributing guilt, assessing excuses, and distinguishing public crimes from private wrongs; also discusses factors that aggravate or mitigate culpability (presumption of power, premeditation, false teachers, examples of impunity).

rubrics_metrics.name: Punishments and Rewards: Definition and Limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Punishment is a hurt inflicted by public authority for the sake of future good; punishments must not be inflicted without public hearing, nor by usurped power, nor without respect to future good; natural evils are not punishments; various kinds of punishments enumerated (corporeal, capital, ignominy, imprisonment, exile); rewards are salary or grace and must be distinguished from benefits bestowed by fear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hobbes articulates moral and legal constraints on legitimate punishment and the proper aims and forms of reward within governance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conquest and the Right of the Conqueror
rubrics_metrics.description: Conquest is acquisition of sovereignty by victory followed by the conquered people's submission; being overcome (slain, imprisoned) is not the same as being conquered; conquest requires promise of obedience or tacit signs such as living under protection openly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criterion for when victory produces legitimate sovereign authority; clarifies when subjects become obliged to obey post-conquest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Causes of Dissolution of a Commonwealth
rubrics_metrics.description: Causes that weaken or dissolve common-wealths include: lack of absolute power, private judgment of good and evil, erroneous conscience, pretence of inspiration, subjecting sovereign power to civil laws, attributing absolute propriety to subjects, dividing sovereign power, imitation of foreign nations, mixed government, want of money, monopolies, popularity of demagogues, excessive municipal power, liberty of disputing against sovereign power, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hobbes lists institutional and cultural pathologies that threaten stability; useful as evaluative checklist for state fragility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Office and Duties of the Sovereign Representative
rubrics_metrics.description: The sovereign's office is to procure the good of the people by instruction and laws; duties include seeing to education of subjects about their duties, maintaining public order, enacting laws that are necessary and perspicuous, providing punishments and rewards, appointing counsellors and commanders, managing public taxes and charity, and preventing idleness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specifies positive obligations and programmatic measures a sovereign should implement to secure peace and welfare.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power Ecclesiastical and Limits of Church Authority
rubrics_metrics.description: Ecclesiastical power is primarily power to teach; civil sovereign holds authority over many ecclesiastical matters in his dominions; pastors and church officers in a Christian common-wealth are subject to civil sovereign, who may appoint pastors and exercise pastoral functions; excommunication has limited civil effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hobbes outlines the proper relation between church and state, arguing for substantial civil control over religious offices and teaching to preserve peace and uniformity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scripture, Prophecy, and Criteria for Religious Authority
rubrics_metrics.description: Marks of a true prophet include miracles and doctrine conformable to law; miracles are rare and must be examined; prophecy (outside sovereign prophet) is to be examined by subjects; scripture supplies authority after the ceasing of ordinary prophetic testimony; interpretation of scripture must be constrained by reason and civil order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides normative tests for accepting prophetic or scriptural claims and links religious authority to civil stability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Signification and Use of Terms: Definitions and Method
rubrics_metrics.description: Hobbes systematically defines key terms (sense, imagination, reason, law, covenant, person, right, liberty, etc.) and emphasizes the method of deriving political doctrine from human nature and passions; clear definition and consistent use of terms are necessary for philosophical and political clarity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An explicit methodological rubric: start from definitions and human nature, use clear language, and avoid relying solely on antiquity or authority when arguing political principles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Property and Distribution: Sovereign's Prerogative
rubrics_metrics.description: All private estates of land originally proceed from the arbitrary distribution of the sovereign; propriety of a subject does not exclude sovereign dominion; the sovereign determines places and matters of traffic and laws of transferring property; money is the 'blood' of a common-wealth and its conduits are public concern.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hobbes locates the legal basis of property rights in sovereign will and public regulation; useful for assessing legitimacy of property regimes and fiscal policy.
